messages.content:
category | variance_cents | variance_pct
Dining out | 18600 | 93
Fun | -4800 | -24
Groceries | 4500 | 7.5
Transport | -900 | -3.6
Subscriptions | -162 | -0.9

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(actual_cents) - SUM(budgeted_cents) AS net_variance FROM household

messages.content: The month nets to 17238 cents over plan, and the pack's one number is this: dining out's overrun of 18600 cents is 107.9% of the entire net variance - the leak is bigger than the flood, because the rest of the household netted to a small saving. Fun came in 4800 under, transport 900 under, subscriptions 162 under; groceries ran 4500 over; housing and the savings transfer hit plan to the cent - and note the savings transfer happening in full is what makes this a loose month rather than a damaging one: the household overspent its consumption plan but did not raid its future to do it. The action the pack supports is narrow and specific: a conversation about dining - its plan (20000, against an actual that has clearly outgrown it) or its frequency - and nothing else. No general tightening, no guilt about groceries. That narrowness is the pack's whole value: a household that responds to a +17238 month by scrutinizing every category teaches itself to ignore the pack; a household that fixes one named leak per month compounds.
Our repairs line is way over budget and rent looks oddly under. I think something's posted to the wrong line. Can you hunt for it?

Misclassification has a fingerprint: the vendor. A line whose entries include a vendor that belongs to another line is guilty until proven innocent. Here are the quarter's actuals with vendors exposed:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE actuals (entry TEXT PRIMARY KEY, line TEXT NOT NULL, vendor TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO actuals VALUES ('A1', 'Repairs', 'FixIt Plumbing', 42000), ('A2', 'Repairs', 'Park Ave Properties LLC', 165000), ('A3', 'Repairs', 'ToolHire Depot', 18000), ('A4', 'Rent', 'Park Ave Properties LLC', 165000), ('A5', 'Rent', 'Park Ave Properties LLC', 165000)
SELECT entry, line, vendor, amount_cents FROM actuals WHERE line = 'Repairs' AND vendor = 'Park Ave Properties LLC'

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
entry | line | vendor | amount_cents
A2 | Repairs | Park Ave Properties LLC | 165000

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS repairs_as_posted FROM actuals WHERE line = 'Repairs'
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS repairs_corrected FROM actuals WHERE line = 'Repairs' AND vendor != 'Park Ave Properties LLC'
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS rent_corrected FROM actuals WHERE vendor = 'Park Ave Properties LLC'

messages.content: Found it. Entry A2 is 165000 cents from Park Ave Properties LLC - your landlord - posted to Repairs. As posted, Repairs totals 225000 against a 90000 plan, a terrifying +150% overrun; corrected, repairs are 60000 (plumbing 42000 plus tool hire 18000), comfortably under plan. Meanwhile Rent showed only two payments because the third was hiding in Repairs; the landlord's true total is 495000 - exactly three months at 165000, exactly on plan. Both variances were fiction, in opposite directions, from a single mis-posted entry. The pattern to institutionalize: a monthly exception report listing entries whose vendor's usual line differs from the line posted - vendors are creatures of habit, and a landlord in Repairs or a plumber in Travel is almost always a keying error. Correct the entry by reclassification (never by deleting and re-entering, which breaks the audit trail), and note that every decision made from the uncorrected variances - including any scolding the repairs budget holder received - needs revisiting.
Our software spend looks double-counted in the spring. Can you check the actuals for the same invoice appearing twice?
Duplicate detection is a grouping query: any invoice number with more than one entry is a suspect, and the amounts will usually match to the cent:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE actuals (entry TEXT PRIMARY KEY, invoice_no TEXT NOT NULL, line TEXT NOT NULL, period TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT invoice_no, COUNT(*) AS entries, SUM(amount_cents) AS total_cents FROM actuals GROUP BY invoice_no HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS spring_as_reported FROM actuals
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) - 84500 AS spring_corrected FROM actuals

messages.content: Invoice INV-2214 appears twice: entry E-301 in March and E-317 in April, 84500 cents each time. The spring total as reported is 281749 cents; corrected for the duplicate it is 197249 - the budget view was overstating software spend by exactly one invoice. Note the trap in entry E-310: it is also 84500, but under a different invoice number (INV-2231) - a legitimate recurring charge at the same price. Duplicates are identified by invoice number (ideally number plus vendor), never by amount alone; an amount-only sweep would have deleted a real payment and 'fixed' the total by a second error. How it usually happens: the invoice was paid in March, then re-entered in April from a reminder email or a scanned copy. The system fix is a uniqueness rule on invoice number per vendor at entry time - cheap to enforce, and this query becomes the monthly backstop. If the duplicate was also PAID twice, that is a recovery conversation with the vendor, armed with both entry records.

Help - my variance report says software is over budget by nine thousand percent. The plan was loaded from a spreadsheet where I typed dollar amounts, but actuals are in cents. Can you confirm that's the problem and repair the comparison?

A variance of +9837% is not a spending event; it is a unit error announcing itself. The diagnostic: if actual divided by plan comes out near 100 on line after line, the plan is in dollars and the actuals in cents:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE lines (line TEXT PRIMARY KEY, planned_typed INTEGER NOT NULL, actual_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO lines VALUES ('Software', 2400, 238500), ('Rent', 15000, 1500000), ('Travel', 5200, 487000), ('Training', 1800, 171000)
SELECT line, planned_typed, actual_cents, ROUND(actual_cents * 1.0 / planned_typed, 1) AS ratio FROM lines ORDER BY ratio DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
line | planned_typed | actual_cents | ratio
Rent | 15000 | 1500000 | 100
Software | 2400 | 238500 | 99.4
Training | 1800 | 171000 | 95
Travel | 5200 | 487000 | 93.7

arguments.sql: SELECT line, planned_typed * 100 AS planned_cents, actual_cents, actual_cents - planned_typed * 100 AS variance_cents FROM lines ORDER BY line

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
line | planned_cents | actual_cents | variance_cents
Rent | 1500000 | 1500000 | 0
Software | 240000 | 238500 | -1500
Training | 180000 | 171000 | -9000
Travel | 520000 | 487000 | -33000

arguments.sql: SELECT ROUND(MAX(actual_cents * 1.0 / planned_typed), 1) AS max_ratio FROM lines

messages.content: Confirmed. The ratios cluster right around 100 - software at 99.4, rent at exactly 100.0, training at 95.0, travel at 93.7 (the 100 maximum) - the signature of a dollars-versus-cents mismatch, not of spending. Repaired by scaling the plan by 100, the true variances are modest and plausible: software is 1500 UNDER its 240000 plan, rent is exactly on plan at 1500000, travel is 33000 under, and training 9000 under. The quarter was actually well controlled; the report was the only thing out of control. Three lessons worth banking. Unit errors produce absurd percentages, so any variance beyond a few hundred percent should be treated as a data defect until proven otherwise - real spending almost never does that. Mixed-unit loads are prevented at the door: the plan table should carry its unit in its name or schema (planned_cents), and a load-time check that plan and actual magnitudes are comparable would have caught this in seconds. And never repair by scaling the ACTUALS down - the actuals are the system of record in cents; the plan conforms to them, not the reverse.
Utilities is showing a lovely year-to-date saving, but I have a nagging feeling March is just... absent. Can you check whether every month actually has actuals?
A missing month and a zero-spend month look identical in a naive sum - and opposite in reality. The check is a calendar table joined against the actuals, so absence becomes visible:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE months (month_no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, month TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO months VALUES (1, 'Jan'), (2, 'Feb'), (3, 'Mar'), (4, 'Apr'), (5, 'May')
CREATE TABLE actuals (month_no INTEGER NOT NULL, line TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO actuals VALUES (1, 'Utilities', 96500), (2, 'Utilities', 91200), (4, 'Utilities', 99800), (5, 'Utilities', 94300)
SELECT m.month, a.amount_cents FROM months m LEFT JOIN actuals a ON a.month_no = m.month_no AND a.line = 'Utilities' ORDER BY m.month_no

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
month | amount_cents
Jan | 96500
Feb | 91200
Mar | NULL
Apr | 99800
May | 94300

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS missing_months FROM months m LEFT JOIN actuals a ON a.month_no = m.month_no AND a.line = 'Utilities' WHERE a.amount_cents IS NULL
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS reported_ytd FROM actuals WHERE line = 'Utilities'

messages.content: Your nagging feeling is correct: 1 month - March - has no utilities actuals at all. The year-to-date total of 381800 cents is the sum of four months being compared against five months of plan (475000), manufacturing a fake saving of 93200 that is mostly just the absent March. The likely truth is mundane: a bill that arrived late, a direct debit that failed, or an accrual nobody posted - the spend almost certainly happened; the record did not. Until March is found, the correct report is not 'utilities saved 93200' but 'utilities actuals are incomplete: four of five months present'. The standing defenses: every actuals table gets a completeness check against the calendar before any variance is computed (the LEFT JOIN above, run for every line, not just the suspicious one), and missing months are reported as a data-quality line in the pack itself. A variance computed on incomplete data is worse than no variance, because it points management attention - and sometimes bonuses - in a direction reality never went.
We retired the 'Legacy hosting' line at the end of last year and moved everything to 'Cloud hosting'. Cloud looks suspiciously cheap this year. Is money still landing on the dead line?
Retired lines that still accept postings are a classic leak: the money goes somewhere the reports no longer look. Checking actuals against line status:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE lines (line TEXT PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO lines VALUES ('Cloud hosting', 'active'), ('Legacy hosting', 'retired'), ('Software', 'active')
CREATE TABLE actuals (entry TEXT PRIMARY KEY, line TEXT NOT NULL, period TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO actuals VALUES ('H1', 'Cloud hosting', '2026-01', 88000), ('H2', 'Cloud hosting', '2026-02', 89500), ('H3', 'Cloud hosting', '2026-03', 90200), ('H4', 'Legacy hosting', '2026-01', 38500), ('H5', 'Legacy hosting', '2026-02', 38500), ('H6', 'Legacy hosting', '2026-03', 38500)
SELECT a.entry, a.period, a.amount_cents FROM actuals a JOIN lines l ON l.line = a.line WHERE l.status = 'retired' ORDER BY a.period
SELECT SUM(a.amount_cents) AS posted_to_retired FROM actuals a JOIN lines l ON l.line = a.line WHERE l.status = 'retired'
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) + 115500 AS cloud_true_total FROM actuals WHERE line = 'Cloud hosting'

messages.content: Yes - 115500 cents has landed on the retired Legacy hosting line this year: 38500 in each of January, February, and March, the unmistakable rhythm of a standing charge nobody redirected when the lines were reorganized. Cloud hosting's true cost is 383200 cents for the quarter, not the 267700 showing on its own line - so its flattering variance against plan was the mirror image of the dead line's invisible spend. Two separate failures made this possible: the vendor's payment details still pointed at the old cost code, and the retired line was retired in name only - the system still accepted postings to it. Retirement must be a system state, not a memo: a retired line rejects new entries, and any standing charge pointing at it fails loudly at the first attempt rather than silently for a quarter. Add the join above to the monthly checks - actuals on non-active lines should be a permanent zero, and the month it is not zero, you have found either a keying error or, as here, a process that never actually changed.
Our materials line looks 136000 under budget, which seems too good. I remember a big returns credit somewhere in there. Can you split the line into gross spend and credits?
A credit note netted inside a spend line flatters the variance and hides the gross truth. Splitting the line by sign:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE actuals (entry TEXT PRIMARY KEY, kind TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO actuals VALUES ('M-01', 'invoice', 186000), ('M-02', 'invoice', 174000), ('M-03', 'invoice', 152000), ('M-04', 'credit note - returned stock', -148000)
SELECT CASE WHEN amount_cents >= 0 THEN 'gross spend' ELSE 'credits' END AS stream, SUM(amount_cents) AS total_cents, COUNT(*) AS entries FROM actuals GROUP BY stream

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
stream | total_cents | entries
credits | -148000 | 1
gross spend | 512000 | 3

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS gross_spend FROM actuals WHERE amount_cents >= 0
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS net_spend FROM actuals

messages.content: The split tells a different story from the net. Gross materials spend is 512000 cents - actually 12000 OVER the 500000 plan. A single credit note of -148000 for returned stock then nets the line down to 364000, manufacturing the apparent 136000 saving. Neither the gross nor the net alone is the truth: the gross tells you purchasing ran slightly hot; the credit tells you 148000 of what was bought came back - which is its own finding, because returns at 29% of gross purchases suggest an ordering problem (wrong specification, over-ordering, a quality failure) that the flattering net variance was concealing. Reporting rule: spend lines are reported gross, with credits shown as their own line beneath, and variance is judged on the gross against plan while credits are reviewed separately for what they reveal. Netting is legitimate in the ledger's arithmetic and corrosive in management reporting - the same reason refunds are not netted against revenue in any serious sales report. If returns recur monthly, they graduate to a planned line of their own with its own target: reduce the returns, not just record them.
Every line in my budget shows a small variance - a few thousand cents either way - and my team keeps trying to explain them. I typed the plan amounts as round numbers. Are we chasing rounding?
Almost certainly. If the plan was rounded to the nearest 10000 cents, then any variance smaller than half that unit - 5000 - is indistinguishable from the rounding itself:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE lines (line TEXT PRIMARY KEY, planned_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, actual_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO lines VALUES ('Stationery', 120000, 118450), ('Postage', 80000, 82310), ('Tea and kitchen', 45000, 44920), ('Printing', 60000, 58150), ('Courier', 30000, 31480)
SELECT line, actual_cents - planned_cents AS variance_cents FROM lines ORDER BY ABS(actual_cents - planned_cents) DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
line | variance_cents
Postage | 2310
Printing | -1850
Stationery | -1550
Courier | 1480
Tea and kitchen | -80

arguments.sql: SELECT MAX(ABS(actual_cents - planned_cents)) AS largest_abs_variance FROM lines

messages.content: The largest absolute variance on the table is 2310 cents - stationery at -1550, postage at +2310, courier at +1480, printing at -1850, tea at -80. Every one of them sits far inside the 5000-cent rounding band of your typed plan, which means none of them contains any information: the plan said 'about 120000' and the actual was 118450, and the difference is the sound of the word 'about'. Chasing these as performance is worse than a waste of a meeting - it teaches the team that the numbers are noise, and they will apply that lesson later to a variance that matters. Two fixes, one for each direction. For small lines, keep the round plan but adopt a materiality threshold in the report itself: variances under the threshold are listed without commentary, by design. For large lines, plan at full precision from the underlying build-up (contracts, headcount, rates) so the variance means something. The general principle: a variance deserves an explanation only when it exceeds the precision of the plan that produced it.

Our combined 'Salaries' line shows a small +30000 variance, but the Sales director swears her salaries are under and the Ops director admits his are over. The report groups by line name only. Can you separate them?
Both directors are right, and the report is wrong: 'Salaries' is two different budgets sharing a name, and grouping by name nets a good story against a bad one:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE lines (department TEXT NOT NULL, line TEXT NOT NULL, planned_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, actual_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO lines VALUES ('Sales', 'Salaries', 2400000, 2350000), ('Ops', 'Salaries', 3100000, 3180000), ('Sales', 'Travel', 400000, 462000), ('Ops', 'Materials', 1500000, 1445000)
SELECT line, SUM(actual_cents) - SUM(planned_cents) AS name_only_variance FROM lines GROUP BY line
SELECT department, line, actual_cents - planned_cents AS variance_cents FROM lines WHERE line = 'Salaries' ORDER BY department

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
department | line | variance_cents
Ops | Salaries | 80000
Sales | Salaries | -50000

Grouped by name alone, Salaries shows +30000 - a rounding-sized shrug. Separated by department, Sales salaries are -50000 (under plan, as the Sales director said) and Ops salaries are +80000 (over, as the Ops director admitted): two real stories of opposite sign, netting into a fiction of calm. The +30000 is not an average of their performance; it is the cancellation of it, and a manager reading only the combined line would congratulate and scold the wrong people in the wrong proportions. The rule is structural: a budget line's identity is department PLUS line name, always - the pair is the key, in the table and in every grouping. This failure mode grows with the organization: the day a third department adds its own 'Salaries', 'Software', or 'Travel', every name-only report silently becomes a blend. If leadership wants a company-wide salaries total, it should be produced as a deliberate rollup labeled as such - a sum for context - never as the line against which any individual department is judged.
March legal was reported as 8000 under budget and we closed the month. Now a late invoice has appeared and someone says March was actually over. Can you show me both versions of March?
A closed month is a snapshot, not a law of nature: late postings restate it, and the honest pack shows the restatement explicitly rather than letting two versions of March circulate:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE entries (entry TEXT PRIMARY KEY, service_month TEXT NOT NULL, posted_date TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS march_as_closed FROM entries WHERE service_month = '2026-03' AND posted_date <= '2026-04-15'
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS march_restated FROM entries WHERE service_month = '2026-03'

messages.content: Both versions exist and both are documented. As closed in mid-April, March legal totaled 112000 cents - the two entries posted by then - which against the 120000 plan was the reported 8000 under. The late invoice L-03, for March work but posted on 19 May, restates March to 159000: actually 39000 OVER plan. The favorable variance the business acted on in April was an artifact of the invoice's journey, not of legal's spending. The mature handling is procedural: closed months are reported as-reported (the snapshot is preserved, because decisions were made from it), restatements are shown as a separate bridge line in the next pack ('March legal restated +47000: late invoice L-03'), and chronic lateness from one supplier becomes a procurement conversation about their invoicing, not a monthly surprise. What you must never do is silently overwrite the closed figure - the first time a manager catches a historical number changing without a bridge, every other number in the pack loses its credibility, including the true ones.

Our Berlin office line is planned in US dollars but the actuals come in euros - 342000 euro cents against a 400000 dollar-cent plan. The naive variance says we're 58000 under. The rate is 1 euro = 1.08 dollars. What's the real variance?
Comparing across currencies without converting is a unit error wearing a nicer suit than most. Convert the actuals at the stated rate, then compare:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE actuals (entry TEXT PRIMARY KEY, currency TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS eur_total FROM actuals

messages.content: The Berlin office spent 342000 euro cents. Converted at 1.08, that is 369360 US dollar cents - so the true variance against the 400000 plan is -30640: a genuine saving of 30640, not the -58000 the naive comparison claims. The naive figure overstates the saving by 27360 cents, which is pure exchange-rate illusion. Two disciplines follow for any multi-currency budget. The conversion rate must be a stated, dated input to the report - budget rate, month-end rate, or actual transaction rates are all defensible choices, but the choice is part of the numbers' meaning, and mixing rates between months makes trends unreadable. And a variance on a foreign line should ideally be split into an operating part (what the Berlin team controlled, measured in euros against a euro plan) and a currency part (what the exchange rate did) - because holding a local manager accountable for the euro's movement is the FX version of blaming the repairs line for a mis-posted rent payment. Convert first, judge second.

Before our budget data goes to the auditors, run me a data-quality sweep over the actuals: duplicates, postings to retired lines, missing months, and credit notes hiding inside spend lines. One dataset, four checks.
The sweep as four mechanical checks over the same tables, each returning its findings with amounts so the issues can be sized, not just counted:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE lines (line TEXT PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO lines VALUES ('Materials', 'active'), ('Utilities', 'active'), ('Legacy ads', 'retired')
CREATE TABLE actuals (entry TEXT PRIMARY KEY, line TEXT NOT NULL, month_no INTEGER NOT NULL, invoice_no TEXT, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT invoice_no, COUNT(*) AS entries FROM actuals WHERE invoice_no IS NOT NULL GROUP BY invoice_no HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
SELECT a.entry, a.line, a.amount_cents FROM actuals a JOIN lines l ON l.line = a.line WHERE l.status = 'retired'

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
entry | line | amount_cents
Q-05 | Legacy ads | 28000

arguments.sql: SELECT CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM actuals WHERE line = 'Utilities' AND month_no = 3) THEN 'present' ELSE 'MISSING' END AS utilities_march
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) - 62000 AS duplicate_amount FROM actuals WHERE invoice_no = 'INV-900'
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS credit_notes_netted FROM actuals WHERE amount_cents < 0

messages.content: The sweep finds four issues, three of them quantifiable. One: invoice INV-900 is entered twice, double-counting 62000 cents of materials spend. Two: entry Q-05 posts 28000 cents to Legacy ads, a retired line - spend the current reports do not see. Three: entry Q-04 is a credit note of -19000 cents netted silently inside Materials, flattering that line's variance. Four - the completeness check - Utilities has January and February actuals but March is MISSING entirely: unquantifiable from the data, and for that reason the most serious finding, because a missing month manufactures a fake saving of unknown size in every report that includes the line. The quantified issues total 109000 cents of distortion. Send the auditors the sweep itself along with the corrections: a dataset that arrives with its own defect list, each defect sized and dispositioned, reads as controlled; a dataset whose defects the auditors find themselves reads as careless - even if the defects are identical. Then make the four checks permanent: they cost one query each, monthly, and they are the difference between discovering your data's problems and being discovered by them.
We always plan one number and then act surprised. Build me a three-case plan for next year - downside, base, upside - and tell me the swing I should actually be managing.
A single-point plan hides the only thing that matters: how wide the range of plausible years is. Three composed cases, same cost discipline, different demand:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE cases (case_name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, costs_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT case_name, revenue_cents, costs_cents, revenue_cents - costs_cents AS profit_cents FROM cases ORDER BY profit_cents

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
case_name | revenue_cents | costs_cents | profit_cents
Downside | 8200000 | 7900000 | 300000
Base | 9600000 | 8300000 | 1300000
Upside | 10900000 | 8800000 | 2100000

arguments.sql: SELECT MAX(revenue_cents - costs_cents) - MIN(revenue_cents - costs_cents) AS profit_swing FROM cases

messages.content: The three cases profit at 300000 (downside), 1300000 (base), and 2100000 (upside) - a swing of 1800000 cents between a plausible bad year and a plausible good one. Notice the asymmetry the cases expose: revenue falls 1400000 from base to downside but costs only give back 400000, because most of the cost base is fixed - rent, salaries, and contracts do not care about demand. That operating leverage is the real content of the table: it says a 15% revenue miss does not produce a 15% profit miss, it produces a 77% one. Managing the swing means working on the asymmetry before the year starts: which of the fixed costs could be made variable (contractors instead of hires, revenue-share instead of flat rent), and how much downside profit each conversion buys. The cases also discipline the upside: at 2100000 the plan should already say what the surplus does - hires, debt paydown, reserves - because windfalls without a pre-written destination get spent at the speed of enthusiasm. One number is a hope; three numbers are a plan.
Our plan: price 2500 cents, volume 4000 units, fixed costs 6000000, variable cost 600 a unit. Four things could move 10% - price, volume, fixed costs, unit cost. Which one should I lose sleep over?
Sensitivity analysis answers that by moving one input at a time by the same percentage and ranking the damage. Base profit first, then each swing:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE model (input TEXT PRIMARY KEY, base_value INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO model VALUES ('price_cents', 2500), ('volume_units', 4000), ('fixed_cents', 6000000), ('unit_cost_cents', 600)

messages.content: Base profit is 1600000 cents. A 10% move in each input, one at a time: price swings profit by 1000000 cents - the full 10% of revenue lands on profit because costs do not move with price. Volume swings it by 760000: extra units bring their contribution (price minus unit cost), not their full price. Fixed costs swing it by 600000, and unit cost by only 240000 - 10% of a 600-cent cost across 4000 units. The ranking is price, then volume, then fixed costs, then unit cost - and it inverts most managers' instincts, which fixate on costs because costs feel controllable. The implication is not 'ignore costs' but 'defend price first': a 10% price concession given away in negotiation destroys more profit than a 10% rise in your unit cost, and recovering it through volume requires over 500 additional units - 1000000 cents of extra contribution at 1900 a unit - just to stand still. Sensitivity tables earn their keep by redirecting anxiety toward the input that actually governs the outcome.
Our budget plans 4200 units at 3000 cents each, variable cost 1800 a unit, fixed costs 4500000. Where's break-even, and how much room do we have?
Break-even is fixed costs divided by the contribution each unit makes - the volume at which the plan crosses zero, and the reference point every volume discussion should start from:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE plan (item TEXT PRIMARY KEY, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO plan VALUES ('price', 3000), ('variable_cost', 1800), ('fixed_costs', 4500000), ('planned_units', 4200)

messages.content: Each unit contributes 1200 cents toward fixed costs, so break-even sits at 3750 units. The plan's 4200 units clear it by 450 units - a margin of safety of 10.7% - and produce a planned profit of 540000 cents. Read those two numbers together: the entire year's profit is generated by the last 450 units sold, and a volume shortfall of just 10.7% - a mediocre quarter, a lost client, a slow season running long - erases the profit completely while leaving revenue looking 89% healthy. That is the number to carry into every decision the plan touches. A discount that trades price for volume must be judged against it (cutting price to 2800 drops contribution to 1000 and pushes break-even to 4500 units - above the current plan, so the 'growth' discount would need volume the plan does not contain). And fixed-cost additions are break-even additions: every 120000 of new fixed cost raises the crossing point by 100 units that must be sold before the year earns anything.

If revenue dips mid-year I don't want to invent cuts in a panic. Can you build our cut list now, in priority order, with cumulative savings - so we know in advance how deep we have to go to close a 500000-cent gap?

A cut list written in calm weather is a different instrument from one written in a crisis: the order reflects strategy rather than whoever is in the room. With cumulative savings, the depth needed for any gap size is read straight off:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE cuts (priority INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, item TEXT NOT NULL, saving_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, note TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO cuts VALUES (1, 'Freeze contractor spend', 240000, 'reversible in a week'), (2, 'Pause events and sponsorships', 180000, 'reversible next quarter'), (3, 'Renegotiate software contracts', 95000, 'needs 60 days notice'), (4, 'Reduce travel to essential only', 140000, 'some client impact'), (5, 'Defer two planned hires', 600000, 'growth impact - last resort')
SELECT priority, item, saving_cents, SUM(saving_cents) OVER (ORDER BY priority) AS cumulative_cents FROM cuts ORDER BY priority

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
priority | item | saving_cents | cumulative_cents
1 | Freeze contractor spend | 240000 | 240000
2 | Pause events and sponsorships | 180000 | 420000
3 | Renegotiate software contracts | 95000 | 515000
4 | Reduce travel to essential only | 140000 | 655000
5 | Defer two planned hires | 600000 | 1255000

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(saving_cents) AS total_cut_capacity FROM cuts

messages.content: The list holds 1255000 cents of total capacity, and the cumulative column is the decision tool: a 500000-cent gap is closed by the first THREE cuts alone - contractor freeze, events pause, software renegotiation - reaching 515000 without touching travel or, critically, the hires. The ordering encodes values the panic version never gets right: reversibility first (the contractor freeze can be undone in a week when revenue recovers), notice periods respected (software renegotiation needs 60 days, which is why it sits at priority 3 rather than lower - if a gap looks likely, that one starts early), and the growth-damaging cut - deferring hires, the largest single saving at 600000 - held last despite its size, because taking it first in a panic is how a one-year dip becomes a two-year hole. Review the list quarterly while nothing is wrong: prices change, contracts renew, and a cut list whose savings figures have rotted is a false comfort. The document's real product is not the savings; it is the absence of a crisis meeting.
Take our three cases - downside profit 300000, base 1300000, upside 2100000 - and weight them 25/50/25. What's the expected year, and how should I read it against the base case?
Weighting the cases turns three stories into one planning number - and the comparison with the base case carries information of its own:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE cases (case_name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, profit_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, probability REAL NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO cases VALUES ('Downside', 300000, 0.25), ('Base', 1300000, 0.50), ('Upside', 2100000, 0.25)
SELECT case_name, profit_cents, probability, ROUND(profit_cents * probability) AS contribution_cents FROM cases ORDER BY profit_cents

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
case_name | profit_cents | probability | contribution_cents
Downside | 300000 | 0.25 | 75000
Base | 1300000 | 0.5 | 650000
Upside | 2100000 | 0.25 | 525000

The expected value is 1250000 cents: the downside contributes 75000, the base 650000, the upside 525000. Note that the expected year (1250000) is WORSE than the base case (1300000) despite symmetric probabilities - because the downside is further from base (-1000000) than the upside is (+800000). That asymmetry, operating leverage again, means a business with this case shape should plan its commitments - hires, leases, debt - against something closer to the expected value than to the base, and treat base-case outcomes as mildly good luck rather than entitlement. Two warnings about the instrument. The probabilities are judgments wearing the costume of data; their honest use is to force the conversation 'how likely is the downside, really?' into the open, not to manufacture precision. And the expected value is a number no actual year will produce - the year will be one of the cases, or outside them entirely. Its job is calibration of commitments, not prediction. Budget to the base, commit to the expected, and keep the cut list sized to the downside.
Show me profit across volumes from 3000 to 6000 units in steps of 500 - price 2500, variable cost 900, fixed 5500000. I want to see where we cross zero, not just be told.
A grid computed in one query - profit as a function of volume, so the crossing point is visible in the shape of the table:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE volumes (units INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)
SELECT units, units * (2500 - 900) - 5500000 AS profit_cents FROM volumes ORDER BY units

messages.content: The grid walks from -700000 at 3000 units through zero between 3000 and 3500, up to 4100000 at 6000 - each 500-unit step worth exactly 800000 cents, the contribution of 1600 a unit made visible as the table's rhythm. The exact crossing is 3438 units: below it the year loses money no matter how well costs are managed, because the fixed base simply is not covered. Two readings matter more than the crossing itself. The slope is the strategy: at 1600 cents of contribution, every commercial argument is really an argument about moving one row down this table - a marketing proposal should be required to name the row it credibly reaches, and a volume forecast is a claim about a row, not a number in isolation. And the margin in concrete units: a plan at 4500 units (profit 1700000) sits 1062 units above the crossing - 'how wrong can we be before we lose money' answered as a distance, a question the single-point plan could not even phrase. Keep the grid next to the budget; it converts anxiety into geography.

Stress our summer cash plan: opening balance 300000, base monthly nets of +120000, +90000, +150000 for July to September. In the downside those become -45000, -75000, +15000. Where does cash bottom out in each world?
The stress test runs both worlds through the same running-balance machinery, because the question is never the total - it is the lowest point the balance touches on the way:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE stress (month_no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, month TEXT NOT NULL, base_net INTEGER NOT NULL, downside_net INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT month, 300000 + SUM(base_net) OVER (ORDER BY month_no) AS base_balance, 300000 + SUM(downside_net) OVER (ORDER BY month_no) AS downside_balance FROM stress ORDER BY month_no

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
month | base_balance | downside_balance
Jul | 420000 | 255000
Aug | 510000 | 180000
Sep | 660000 | 195000

arguments.sql: SELECT MIN(bal) AS downside_low_point FROM (SELECT 300000 + SUM(downside_net) OVER (ORDER BY month_no) AS bal FROM stress)
SELECT MIN(bal) AS base_low_point FROM (SELECT 300000 + SUM(base_net) OVER (ORDER BY month_no) AS bal FROM stress)

messages.content: In the base world the balance climbs from 420000 to 660000 - its low point is July's 420000. In the downside world it falls through 255000 in July to a low of 180000 cents in August, recovering only slightly to 195000 in September. The quarter's total swing between worlds is 465000, but the number that governs decisions is the August low: 180000 is survivable - no floor breached, no credit line needed - yet it is 330000 below where the base plan's August sits, and it arrives precisely when a business is least able to raise money quickly. The stress test's output should be actions dated before the stress: if the downside low point had come out negative, the responses (arranging the credit line in June while the balance sheet looks strong, pulling a discretionary spend out of August, tightening July's receivables push) all live in the calm months. A cash plan without a downside twin is only a description of the year you hope for; the pair of them is a plan.

Our plan has a trigger: if Q1 revenue hits 110% of its 5500000 plan, we hire the support engineer from Q2 at 780000 a year. Q1 revenue came in at 6180000. Did the trigger fire, and what does it do to the year?
Trigger-based plans are scenarios with the decision pre-made - but the trigger must be checked against the threshold exactly, not vibes:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE trigger_check (item TEXT PRIMARY KEY, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO trigger_check VALUES ('Q1 revenue plan', 5500000), ('Q1 revenue actual', 6180000)

messages.content: The threshold is 6050000 cents and actual Q1 revenue beat it by 130000 - the trigger has fired, cleanly, not on a rounding edge. The hire therefore enters the plan from Q2: nine months of cost this year, 585000 cents, against the full 780000 run-rate the plan must carry next year. This is the trigger mechanism working as designed, and its design virtues are worth naming. The decision was made in January's calm, with the criterion written down, so April's conversation is arithmetic rather than politics - nobody has to argue whether the quarter 'feels' strong enough. The criterion is revenue, an input the new hire supports but does not control, so the trigger cannot be gamed by the team that benefits from it. And the plan should carry the symmetrical trigger nobody writes: if Q3 revenue falls below 90% of plan, a named set of costs pauses automatically. Triggers in both directions convert the annual plan from a document into a control system - most budgets only ever install the accelerator.
Build me a two-way sensitivity: profit at prices 2400, 2500, 2600 against volumes 3600, 4000, 4400 - variable cost 600, fixed 6000000. I want the whole grid, then your reading.
Two-way grids show interactions a one-way ranking cannot - especially whether the bad corner stays survivable:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE grid (price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, volume_units INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT price_cents, volume_units, volume_units * (price_cents - 600) - 6000000 AS profit_cents FROM grid ORDER BY price_cents, volume_units

messages.content: The grid's nine cells run from 480000 in the worst corner (price 2400, volume 3600) to 2800000 in the best (2600, 4400), with the plan's base cell - 2500 and 4000 - at 1600000. The first reading is relief with information in it: even the worst corner stays profitable, so this plan does not have a plausible price-and-volume combination that loses money; the risk conversation can move on to costs and cash. The second reading compares the levers at the base cell: a 100-cent price step is worth 400000 cents of profit, while a 400-unit volume step is worth 760000 - volume is the stronger lever per step as the steps are sized here, which argues for the growth investment over the price rise if only one can be pursued. But steps are not equally hard: 100 cents of price may be one negotiation, while 400 units is a quarter of sales effort. The grid cannot price effort - it can only ensure that when the choice is made, both effects are on the table in the same units, instead of the louder department's intuition winning by default.
Our rent is 165000 a month and the landlord is hinting at an 8% rise at the July renewal. What does that do to this year's budget and to the run-rate?
A mid-year price change splits the year into two regimes - the what-if must respect the effective month rather than smearing the rise across all twelve:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE rent (month_no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, monthly_rent INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(monthly_rent) AS rent_year_total FROM rent

messages.content: The 8% rise is 13200 cents a month, effective July. This year's rent total becomes 2059200 cents against 1980000 on the old rate - an in-year hit of 79200, because only six months carry the new rate. But the number that belongs in next year's plan is the run-rate: 158400 cents a year, every year, compounding into every future renewal negotiation. Confusing those two figures is the classic renewal error - the in-year number looks absorbable (79200 against a full budget), so the rise is waved through, and the run-rate quietly resets the cost base forever. The what-if also has a negotiating use: the landlord's 8% is worth 158400 a year to them, which prices the alternatives - a longer lease at 5%, a break clause, or the moving cost amortized over the term - in the same units. And for the budget itself: the rise enters the reforecast as a named change from July, not as a mysterious deterioration in the property line's variance that someone discovers in September and misattributes to the facilities team.

Assemble our scenario pack for the board: three cases with probabilities for the café group, the expected value, the swing, whether our pre-agreed cuts cover the downside gap, and the one sensitivity that matters.
The pack in one pass - cases, weights, expected value, swing, and the cut coverage check, all from the same composed tables:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE cases (case_name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, costs_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, probability REAL NOT NULL)
SELECT case_name, revenue_cents - costs_cents AS profit_cents, probability FROM cases ORDER BY profit_cents

messages.content:
case_name | profit_cents | probability
Downside | 250000 | 0.3
Base | 650000 | 0.5
Upside | 1100000 | 0.2

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE cuts (item TEXT PRIMARY KEY, saving_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO cuts VALUES ('Contractor freeze', 240000), ('Events pause', 180000), ('Software renegotiation', 95000)
SELECT SUM(saving_cents) AS pre_agreed_cuts FROM cuts

messages.content: The pack reads as follows. Cases: downside profits 250000, base 650000, upside 1100000 - a swing of 850000 cents. Weighted at 30/50/20, the expected value is 620000 cents, below the base case because the downside is both more likely and further away than the upside - commitments should be sized to 620000, not 650000. The resilience check passes: the base-to-downside gap is 400000 cents, and the pre-agreed cut list totals 515000 - the business can close the entire downside gap with decisions already made, without an emergency process. The one sensitivity that matters is the rent renewal: an 8% rise at July costs 158400 a year in run-rate, which is 63% of the downside case's entire profit - a single negotiation outweighs most operational initiatives in the plan, and it should be resourced accordingly. What the pack deliberately omits is a fourth case for catastrophe: the cases are for governing the plausible year, and loading them with tail risks makes all three numbers useless for the decisions actually in front of the board. Plausible range, weighted honestly, cuts pre-agreed, dominant sensitivity named - that is a plan a board can govern with.
Build the one-page summary for our finance meeting: top variances with their causes, nothing else. The figures have to come from the lines table - nobody trusts a summary typed from memory.
The one-pager's discipline is selection: the three largest absolute variances, each carrying its cause from the same table the figures came from, so every number on the page can be traced:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE lines (line TEXT PRIMARY KEY, kind TEXT NOT NULL, planned_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, actual_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, cause TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO lines VALUES ('Revenue', 'revenue', 2400000, 2215000, 'anchor client paused orders in May'), ('Salaries', 'cost', 1180000, 1151000, 'one vacancy held open six weeks'), ('Freelance cover', 'cost', 150000, 238000, 'agency cover for parental leave'), ('Hosting', 'cost', 96000, 95400, ''), ('Travel', 'cost', 210000, 246500, 'two extra client trips')
SELECT line, actual_cents - planned_cents AS variance_cents, cause FROM lines ORDER BY ABS(actual_cents - planned_cents) DESC LIMIT 3

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
line | variance_cents | cause
Revenue | -185000 | anchor client paused orders in May
Freelance cover | 88000 | agency cover for parental leave
Travel | 36500 | two extra client trips

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN kind = 'revenue' THEN actual_cents - planned_cents ELSE planned_cents - actual_cents END) AS profit_variance FROM lines

messages.content: The page leads with revenue: -185000, caused by the anchor client's paused orders - the quarter's story in one line. Then freelance cover at +88000 over plan (parental-leave agency cover: expensive, temporary, and already ended), and travel at +36500 (two extra client trips, which belong in the same conversation as the revenue line, since trips are how the anchor relationship gets repaired). Salaries' -29000 favorable and hosting's -600 sit below the fold as context. The net profit variance across all lines is -279900 cents - the quarter is behind plan, and the page says so in its second breath rather than letting the meeting discover it. The format rules that make one-pagers work: every figure traceable to the table it was queried from (no hand-typed numbers, ever - transcription is where packs go to die), every variance carrying a cause that is a fact rather than an adjective, and a strict limit of three headlines. A pack that reports twelve variances reports none of them; the meeting's job is to decide what to do about two or three things, and the page exists to choose which.

Give me our year-end landing estimate: first half is actual, second half is plan adjusted for the two known changes - a new contract worth 180000 of revenue from September, and a rent rise adding 95000 of cost across the half.
The landing estimate is the plan's honest successor: actuals for the elapsed half, plan for the remainder, and known changes applied as named adjustments rather than buried in a fresh guess:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE halves (period TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, costs_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, basis TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO halves VALUES ('H1', 5650000, 4980000, 'actual'), ('H2', 5900000, 5120000, 'plan')

messages.content: The landing: revenue 11730000 cents, costs 10195000, profit 1535000 - which is 85000 AHEAD of the unadjusted landing of 1450000 (elapsed actuals plus untouched second-half plan). The bridge is exactly the two named changes and nothing else: the new contract adds 180000, the rent rise takes 95000, and the year lands ahead because a named, contracted gain outweighs a named, contracted cost. That composition is what makes a landing estimate governable: every element is either history or a signed fact, and the estimate can be re-run the day any element changes. What it must never contain is an unnamed optimism line - 'expected improvements' or 'management actions' with no contract behind them. The moment a landing estimate includes hope as a component, it stops being an estimate and becomes the reforecast-lowers-the-bar failure in a new costume. Report it as a range if the known changes have uncertainty - the contract is signed, the rent rise is a landlord's hint - but keep every component named.

It's November and departments are asking what happens to unspent budget at year-end. Our rules: training money expires, the equipment fund rolls over (capped at 200000), marketing doesn't carry either way. Show me each line's year-end behavior.
Carryover rules are behavior rules: they decide whether December sees a spending spree or a calm close. Applying each line's rule to its unspent balance:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE lines (line TEXT PRIMARY KEY, rule TEXT NOT NULL, budgeted_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, spent_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO lines VALUES ('Training', 'expires', 240000, 156000), ('Equipment fund', 'rolls over', 600000, 410000), ('Marketing', 'no carry', 300000, 322000)
SELECT line, rule, budgeted_cents - spent_cents AS unspent_cents FROM lines ORDER BY line

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
line | rule | unspent_cents
Equipment fund | rolls over | 190000
Marketing | no carry | -22000
Training | expires | 84000

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(budgeted_cents - spent_cents) AS expiring_total FROM lines WHERE rule = 'expires'
SELECT SUM(budgeted_cents - spent_cents) AS rolling_total FROM lines WHERE rule = 'rolls over'

messages.content: Training has 84000 cents unspent, and under its rule that money vanishes on 31 December - which is precisely why training departments book courses in November that nobody needed in June: the rule pays them to spend, and they respond to the payment. The equipment fund rolls 190000 cents into next year, under its 200000 cap with 10000 of headroom - the rolling rule fits capital money, because equipment needs arrive on their own schedule and forcing them into December buys the wrong kit at the wrong price. Marketing is 22000 OVER spent, so its carryover question is moot in the other direction: no rule carries a deficit here, the overrun is absorbed centrally and argued about once. The design principle: expiry suits genuinely annual consumption (training, events) where underspend means the activity did not happen; rollover suits lumpy, multi-year needs (equipment, major maintenance) where underspend means the need has not arrived YET. The pathology to avoid is the mixed message - expiring rules on lumpy lines, which manufacture December waste, and rolling rules on everything, which let departments accumulate private reserves the center cannot see.
Show me the budget's audit trail for the year so far: who changed which line, when, and what the net effect per line has been. I want to prove the plan hasn't quietly mutated.
The change log is the plan's memory. Summarized by line, with the trail itself available for any entry the summary raises questions about:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE change_log (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, changed_on TEXT NOT NULL, line TEXT NOT NULL, old_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, new_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, changed_by TEXT NOT NULL, reason TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO change_log VALUES (1, '2026-01-12', 'Salaries', 1150000, 1180000, 'A. Patel', 'approved hire brought forward'), (2, '2026-02-03', 'Travel', 200000, 210000, 'J. Osei', 'client trip added'), (3, '2026-03-19', 'Salaries', 1180000, 1165000, 'A. Patel', 'hire start date slipped'), (4, '2026-04-08', 'Hosting', 90000, 96000, 'J. Osei', 'price rise at renewal')
SELECT line, COUNT(*) AS changes, SUM(new_cents - old_cents) AS net_change_cents FROM change_log GROUP BY line ORDER BY changes DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
line | changes | net_change_cents
Salaries | 2 | 15000
Travel | 1 | 10000
Hosting | 1 | 6000

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_changes FROM change_log
SELECT SUM(new_cents - old_cents) AS net_plan_drift FROM change_log

messages.content: The trail shows 4 changes all year, each with a named person, a date, and a reason that refers to a real event. Net drift across the whole plan is 31000 cents: salaries net +15000 (a hire brought forward, then partially slipped back - the two entries together tell the true story that neither tells alone), travel +10000, hosting +6000. This is what plan integrity looks like in evidence: the current plan differs from the approved plan by a small, fully enumerated set of changes, and any manager can pick any line and walk it back to the original through named steps. The contrast case is the budget with no log, where the plan 'has always been' whatever it currently is and every variance discussion founders on disputed history. Two rules keep the trail trustworthy: changes are append-only (a correction is a new entry, never an edit - the salaries pair above is the model), and the reason field is mandatory and specific; 'adjustment' as a reason is a log entry that testifies to nothing. Auditors love this table, but its real audience is next year's planning meeting, which inherits a plan whose every deviation from the original has a name and a story.

Our draft pack claims three things: revenue year-to-date is 4125000, the top cost variance is freelance at +88000, and landing profit is 1535000. Verify each claim against the tables before this goes to the board.
Every pack figure gets traced to its table before the board sees it - claims are checked, not believed. One at a time:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE monthly_revenue (month_no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(revenue_cents) AS revenue_ytd FROM monthly_revenue
CREATE TABLE cost_lines (line TEXT PRIMARY KEY, planned_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, actual_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO cost_lines VALUES ('Freelance', 150000, 238000), ('Travel', 210000, 246500), ('Hosting', 96000, 95400)
SELECT MAX(actual_cents - planned_cents) AS top_cost_variance FROM cost_lines

messages.content: Two claims verify and one does not. Revenue year-to-date is exactly 4125000 - claim confirmed. The top cost variance is 88000 from the freelance line - confirmed. But the landing profit does not trace: its stated components - first-half actual profit 670000, second-half planned profit 780000, known changes +83000 - sum to 1533000, not the claimed 1535000. The pack is wrong by 2000 cents, almost certainly a transcription slip when the figure was typed into the slide. Two thousand cents will not change any board decision, and that is exactly why it must be fixed: a pack caught with one untraced figure teaches the board to discount every figure, including the ones that matter. The rule this exercise institutionalizes is that pack numbers are never typed - they are pasted from query output or, better, generated - and any figure that must be assembled from components is assembled by calculation at pack time, as here. The 2000-cent discrepancy also gets disclosed in the meeting, briefly and without drama: corrections volunteered are credibility; corrections discovered are damage.

The pack's final section is the asks: a new hire at 780000 a year recurring, a software migration at 145000 one-off, and a van replacement at 420000 one-off that saves 96000 a year in maintenance. Present them so the board judges each the right way.
Asks fail when they are presented as one lump. They split by kind - recurring asks are judged against the run-rate they permanently change, one-offs against reserves and payback:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE asks (request TEXT PRIMARY KEY, kind TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO asks VALUES ('Support engineer (recurring salary)', 'recurring', 780000), ('Software migration', 'one-off', 145000), ('Van replacement', 'one-off', 420000)
SELECT kind, SUM(amount_cents) AS total_cents, COUNT(*) AS asks FROM asks GROUP BY kind

messages.content: The asks total 1345000 cents, but that sum is meaningless and the pack should not print it: the recurring ask is 780000 a year FOREVER (it raises the cost base and next year's break-even with it), while the one-offs total 565000 once. Judged properly: the hire is a bet that support demand is permanently higher - its evidence belongs in ticket volumes and churn risk, and its approval should be weighed against the sensitivity table, where fixed costs are the third-largest swing. The migration at 145000 is a pure one-off with no payback claim - judged on risk reduction and the cost of staying. The van is the only ask that pays for itself: at 96000 a year of avoided maintenance its payback is 4.4 years, inside the van's expected life, so it can be approved on arithmetic alone. Presenting the three in one list with one total invites the board to average their merits; presenting them by kind, each with its own test, gets three clean decisions. And every approved ask enters the change log the same day - today's ask is next quarter's plan drift, and it should arrive with its name on it.
Nobody made a big change to this year's plan, yet the current plan totals 10385000 against an approved 10100000. Can you quantify the drift line by line and tell me if I should worry?
Death by a thousand cuts has a measurable shape: many small changes, each defensible, whose accumulation nobody approved. Line by line, original against current:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE plan_versions (line TEXT PRIMARY KEY, original_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, current_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, changes INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT line, current_cents - original_cents AS drift_cents, changes FROM plan_versions WHERE current_cents <> original_cents ORDER BY drift_cents DESC

line | drift_cents | changes
Salaries | 185000 | 2
Software | 38000 | 2
Marketing | 35000 | 1
Travel | 28000 | 1
Other | -1000 | 0

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(current_cents) - SUM(original_cents) AS total_drift FROM plan_versions

messages.content: Total drift is 285000 cents - 2.8% of the approved plan - accumulated over six changes: salaries +185000 across two entries, software +38000 across two, travel +28000, marketing +35000, and one line actually drifting down by 1000. No single change breached any approval threshold, which is exactly how a plan mutates without a decision: thresholds police individual changes, and drift is a property of the pile. Should you worry? The amount is not yet alarming - 2.8% is within the range honest mid-year corrections produce - but the pack should now carry a standing drift line: original plan, current plan, cumulative drift, in every meeting, so the pile is always visible. Set a cumulative trigger as the complement to per-change thresholds: when total drift crosses, say, 5% of the approved plan, the plan returns to the board for re-approval as a whole, however innocent each step was. Variances are then reported against the ORIGINAL plan alongside the current one at that point - because a business that drifts its plan 10% and then reports variances against the drifted version has quietly graded its own homework.

The shapes are unmistakable. Marketing spent 123000 across the quarter, of which December alone was 78000 - a 63.4% December share, more than October and November combined, from a line whose underlying activity has no earthly reason to triple in December. The equipment fund spent 114000 with December at 41000 - a 36.0% share, roughly a third, the signature of spending that happens when the need arises. How to handle the finding matters more than the finding: the question is whether approval happened but was not recorded (a logging failure - fix the record, counsel the habit) or never happened (a governance failure - the change is unauthorized and the plan's integrity has a hole in it). Either way the remedy is not to quietly backfill the field, which would falsify the log; the approver, if they exist, adds a dated confirmation entry, and if they do not, the change goes to the director now for ratification or reversal. Threshold audits like this are cheap, unarguable, and - run monthly rather than annually - they keep the log a control instead of a chronicle of everything that got away.
